title: Hierarchical phase batcher with KV supply throttling for heterogeneous turn lengths
creator: Priya Menon
description:
Summary: We see persistent tail latency regressions and GPU memory fragmentation when serving mixed prompt/response workloads (short prompts with long generations and vice versa). This ticket implements a hierarchical phase-based batching scheduler that treats request lifecycles as distinct phases (pre-fill/prefix, steady-state generation, response flush) and enforces a per-phase KV supply policy to reduce KV cache oversubscription and slab fragmentation.

Problem statement: Continuous batching conflates requests at different lifecycle stages which leads to: 1) KV residency hotspots where long-lived responses pin large KV slabs, 2) inefficient coalescing of short prompt-only requests with long-response streams causing increased latency for short tails, and 3) uneven GPU memory pressure that prevents effective kernel packing and reduces throughput.

Goals:
- Reduce p99 and p999 latency regressions for short-turn requests by 30% in mixed workloads.
- Decrease KV cache evictions and re-materializations by 25% on average for the dataset of customer traffic.
- Improve effective GPU utilization for generation workloads by smoothing slab allocation and enabling denser kernel scheduling.

Design overview:
- Lifecycle phases: classify requests into three lightweight runtime phases: PREFIX (prompt arrival and tokenization), GENERATE (steady-state auto-regressive generation), FLUSH (final tokens + response closure). Classification uses sequence-length heuristics and a sliding-window of emitted tokens.
- Hierarchical queues: maintain per-GPU two-tier queues: hot queue for GENERATE-phase requests and fast-path queue for PREFIX/FLUSH short-turns. The scheduler prioritizes the fast-path queue for low-latency service while coalescing GENERATE-phase work into larger micro-batches.
- KV supply throttling: each slot is assigned a per-phase KV quota (measured in bytes-resident). The quota is adaptive based on recent eviction rate and a running KV pressure score. When a slot exceeds the quota, the scheduler delays new GENERATE micro-batches from that slot and prioritizes flushing short prefixes.
- Soft compaction policy: trigger opportunistic KV compaction when GPU free memory falls below a threshold (configurable). Compaction is incremental and piggybacks on idle kernel cycles to avoid visible latency spikes.
- Admission + fallback: new requests that would immediately exceed per-GPU KV allowance are redirected to a lower-cost model variant (quantized) or queued with a short backoff. This integrates with our existing smart routing policies.

Key hyperparameters (initial):
- prefix_threshold_tokens = 32
- flush_stage_window_ms = 1200
- kv_quota_per_slot_bytes = 64MB (adaptive)
- gpu_free_compact_threshold = 0.12 (12% free memory)
- max_delay_for_kv_throttle_ms = 150

Success metrics & dashboards:
- p50/p95/p99 token latency by phase
- KV eviction rate / re-materialization rate per GPU and per model
- GPU occupancy and kernel packing density
- Requests redirected to fallback model / dropped

Experiment plan:
1) Local simulation: run mixed workload traces (sourced from internal replay of anonymized traffic) in the scheduler simulator to tune kv_quota and max_delay. Link: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/rlw-sim-traces-2026 (design doc and traces).
2) Canary rollout on a dedicated fleet: enable hierarchical queuing + kv throttling on 5% of runtime nodes with canary traffic. Monitor the above metrics with alert windows.
3) A/B test (10% traffic) comparing current continuous-batcher vs hierarchical-phase-batcher for two weeks.

Implementation plan & artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Hierarchical+Phase+Batcher+Design (internal)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8421 (initial queueing + phase classifier)
- Follow-up PR for KV quotas and compaction: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8470
- Load test job definitions: https://ci.redwood.ai/job/runtime-batcher-experiments/

Risks and trade-offs:
- Complexity: additional per-request state increases scheduler code complexity and test surface. We'll mitigate by keeping classifier rules simple and providing an opt-out flag.
- Throughput vs latency: prioritizing short-phase requests may reduce throughput slightly on tails. We'll quantify via A/B and adjust quotas.
- Compaction overhead: poorly tuned compaction can introduce jitter; start with conservative thresholds and observe.

Rollout & rollback:
- Step 0: feature-flagged merges behind runtime config.
- Step 1: internal canary on synthetic load, 48h stability.
- Step 2: gradual increase to 5% production, monitor latency and KV eviction.
- Step 3: 10% A/B for two weeks.
- Rollback: flip feature flag and let long-running slots drain; ensure KV state is preserved in metrics.

Notes: Ensure integration with dedicated autoscaling (Dedicated) so KV quotas consider reserved GPU pools; coordinate with Console team to surface per-route KV pressure metrics.
